title: Camera Movement Terms for AI Video: Dolly, Orbit, Crane — cv.cm
description: Camera movement terms for AI video prompts: dolly, truck, pedestal, orbit, crane, dolly zoom, rack focus and more, with what each looks like and how to phrase it.
h1: What are the camera movement terms for AI video prompts?
answer: Camera movement terms are the film-crew words for how the camera moves: pan and tilt rotate it in place, dolly moves it forward or back, truck moves it sideways, pedestal moves it up or down, and orbit circles the subject. Video models learned these words from captioned footage, so naming one standard move gives you far more control than 'cinematic camera'.

body: Video models learn camera language from captions written about real footage. When a caption says 'slow dolly in on her face', the model links that phrase to a specific pattern of motion: the subject grows in frame and the background shifts a little behind it. A vague phrase like 'dynamic camera' links to everything at once, so you get a random mix.

The terms below are the ones film crews use, and most of them appear in Google's Veo prompt guide. Researchers also treat camera motion as its own control signal: Stable Video Diffusion was shown to work with camera-motion modules, and CameraCtrl adds exact camera paths to text-to-video models. That research exists because text alone gives only rough control. Use the right word, keep it to one move per shot, and expect to make a few takes.

Two pairs are easy to confuse. Pan and tilt rotate the camera on the spot, like turning your head. Truck and pedestal move the whole camera sideways or up and down, like stepping to the side or standing up. Rotating gives a flat sweep; moving gives parallax, where near objects slide past faster than far ones.

body: Notes on the hard ones. A zoom and a dolly in can end on the same framing, but only the dolly shows parallax, so it feels like moving through the space. A dolly zoom combines both at once in opposite directions and is difficult for models; ask for it alone, on a simple subject, and generate several takes. A Dutch angle and POV are framing choices rather than moves, but they are written in the same place in a prompt.
Shot size says how much of the subject fills the frame. It is the first thing to fix in a prompt, because it decides what detail the model has to draw.

body: For AI video, closer shots of faces are usually more stable than wide shots of crowds, because the model has fewer small figures to keep consistent. Hands and fingers look best in close-ups with simple motion, or kept partly out of frame.

head: Angle
Camera position
Effect
rows: At ground level, looking up steeply

body: Angles combine with moves. 'Low angle, slow tracking shot' is a clear instruction; the angle fixes the position and the move fixes the path.

sections.h: How to put a camera move into a prompt

ol: Start with the camera line: shot size, angle, move, speed. Example: `Medium close-up, eye level, slow push-in.`
Name the target of the move: push in on what, orbit around whom, pan from where to where.
Give the move a speed and an end: 'slowly', 'over the full clip', 'stops on her face'.
Describe the subject's action separately, and keep it small if the camera move is big.
Add lens words only if they matter: `shallow depth of field`, `wide-angle lens`, `telephoto compression`.

body.code:
Wide shot, low angle, slow crane up.
A lighthouse on a rocky coast at sunset; waves break on the rocks below.
The camera rises from the rocks to above the lighthouse lamp, ending on a
wide view of the sea. Warm orange light, long shadows, light sea mist.
Audio: waves, wind, seagulls.

body: If you work from a single photo, the move can also be made without a video model. For example, cv.cm's `v` tool estimates depth from a photo and renders a real 3D push, pull, orbit, pan or rise. The camera moves; the subject stays still. That is a quick way to see what each move looks like on your own picture.

ul: Combined moves: 'orbit while craning up and zooming' usually gives a warped or wobbling path. Use one move.
Speed: 'fast' moves can blur or distort faces. Fast moves work better on landscapes and empty spaces.
Zoom vs dolly: many models treat both as 'get closer'. If you need parallax, write 'camera moves forward' as well as 'dolly in'.
Full orbits: a 360-degree orbit asks the model to invent the back of everything. A half circle or a short arc is safer.
Rack focus and dolly zoom: these are optical effects, and results vary from one model to another at the time of writing. Test them before planning a sequence around them.
Handheld: some models add too much shake. Say 'slight' or 'subtle'.

body.note: If a tool offers camera controls as sliders or presets, use them instead of text. A numeric control is followed more exactly than a word.

faq.q: What is the difference between a pan and a truck shot?
faq.a: A pan turns the camera left or right from one fixed spot. A truck moves the whole camera sideways, so near and far objects slide past at different speeds.

faq.q: What is the difference between zoom and dolly?
faq.a: A zoom changes the lens and enlarges the image without moving the camera, so there is no parallax. A dolly moves the camera through space, so the background shifts relative to the subject.

faq.q: What is a dolly zoom used for?
faq.a: It keeps the subject the same size while the background seems to stretch or shrink, which shows shock or a sudden realization. It is also called the vertigo effect.

faq.q: What camera movement makes a scene feel tense?
faq.a: A slow push-in toward a face builds tension, and handheld shake or a Dutch angle adds unease. Keep the subject's action small so the move carries the feeling.

faq.q: What does FPV mean in drone video?
faq.a: FPV means first-person view: the pilot flies with goggles, so the footage is fast, low and swooping. In prompts, 'FPV drone shot' asks for that style, unlike a smooth, high aerial shot.
